title: Hold a Koch v1.1 robot arm up as its power is cut for a repair, and lay it limp in its cradle pose without dropping it
instruction: One of this robot arm's servos has failed and stopped its servo bus, so the arm cannot be driven to a rest pose; its power will be cut for the repair and it will go limp. Hold it up so it does not drop: close both grippers on it, and one second later the power is cut. With both grippers still on it, lay it down in its cradle pose (shoulder lift 0.45, elbow flex 0.8, wrist flex -0.35 rad, the other joints 0) without dropping it, then let go.
context: Technicians who service robot arms power them off for repair, and a powered-down arm built on back-drivable servos cannot hold itself up: Trossen warns that terminating control of its Dynamixel-driven WidowX arms 'while the arms are not in their sleep configurations will cause them to collapse!'. When a failed servo has stopped the bus, the arm cannot be driven to a rest pose first, so the technician takes its weight as the power goes and lays it down by hand. The Koch v1.1 is the open-source arm LeRobot drives as koch_follower (Dynamixel XL430-W250 and XL330-M288, about US$278 of parts plus printed links). Unheld at the cut, its forearm falls and a link passes 0.9 m/s, so both grippers must already hold it, the left on the upper arm and the right on the wrist, and move together so it is set down, not dropped. The nearest task on the board, a patient's limp forearm, moves a single limp link, not a five-joint arm.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the YAM arm bases: x forward, y to the robot's left, heights above the bench top. (1) A Koch v1.1 follower arm (the Koch v1.1 URDF and meshes from jess-moss/koch-v1-1 as fixed in ManiSkill's assets: joint axes, limits, link masses; 0.29 kg with its base, 0.22 kg moving), its base (16 x 8 cm) fixed to the bench with its shoulder pan axis at (30, 16), the arm pointing toward -y, standing in its working pose: shoulder pan 0, shoulder lift 1.2, elbow flex 1.2, wrist flex 0, wrist roll 0 rad (upper arm 69 degrees up, elbow 15.2 cm up over (28, 10.7), forearm level, wrist 15.5 cm up at (28, 0.6)). Its servos hold that pose (a stiff position hold) until both YAM grippers have been closed on the arm for 1 s; then its torque is cut (at 30 s if they never close). Its own gripper is not driven (one rigid body with the wrist roll). (2) Unpowered, each joint is back-driven through its Dynamixel gear train (LeRobot koch_follower: XL430-W250 on the shoulder pan and lift, XL330-M288 on the elbow, wrist flex, wrist roll and gripper; ROBOTIS: 258.5:1 and 288.35:1): static friction 0.03 N m per XL430 and 0.012 N m per XL330, damping 0.02 N m s/rad, rotor inertia at the joint 0.005 and 0.002 kg m2 (all estimates). (3) Grip features: the upper arm is a printed bracket 13 mm thick in the arm's plane and 37 mm wide; the wrist is the wrist-roll XL330 in its bracket, 22 mm thick. In the working pose the left pinch is on the upper arm 6 cm out from the shoulder lift axis, at (30, 14.4), 11.5 cm high; the right on the wrist at (29.6, -1.4), 15.5 cm high. In the cradle pose they are 8.8 cm (left, at y = 10.9) and 5.8 cm (right, at y = -5.9) high. (4) A foam pad 12 x 44 x 2 cm, its long side along y, centred at (32.5, -8): its back edge is 2 cm in front of the pan axis, clear of the base, its near edge at x = 26.5 (so the YAM hands are not over it as they lay the arm low), and it covers where the arm lands if nobody holds it. Three foam blocks on the pad, each 6 cm wide in x at x = 30 and cut to the arm's underside in the cradle pose: under the elbow, 2.5 cm long at y = 5.75, top 7.7 cm above the bench; under the forearm, 3.5 cm at y = 0.25, top 5.6 cm; under the gripper, 4 cm at y = -11, top 3.7 cm. (5) Of the arm's links only the forearm, wrist and gripper collide with the upper arm, the base and the shoulder link. The cradle pose is shoulder lift 0.45, elbow flex 0.8, wrist flex -0.35 rad, the other joints 0: the arm laid forward along its blocks, gripper level. Both YAM arms start at their ready pose, grippers open. On a real rig: a Koch v1.1 follower built from jess-moss/koch-v1-1 (bill of materials US$278, printed parts from its STLs); a script calls LeRobot's DynamixelMotorsBus disable_torque on an operator's button once both grippers hold, the bus stays healthy, and Present_Position is logged at 20 Hz.
scoring: From the arm's own joint readings (its encoders report with torque off; each link point's speed from them by the arm's kinematics). 1/3, caught: when the torque is cut, both grippers are closed on the arm (a point of each finger within 1.5 cm of its surface, the mean points of its two fingers under 6 cm apart). 2/3, laid: also every joint within 10 degrees of the cradle pose at the last moment both grippers held it (a hand that lets go first leaves 1/3), and now, the arm still (under 1 cm/s) and resting on its foam. 1.0, let go: then both whole grippers (fingers, pads, palm, housing and 12 cm of wrist) at least 5 cm from the arm's surface, the arm still laid, for 2 s. A drop voids the run (0): after the cut, any point of the arm faster than 0.5 m/s, or a link striking the bench, pad or foam faster than 0.25 m/s (an unheld arm passes 0.58 m/s within 0.1 s of the cut and peaks at 0.9 m/s).
reset_notes: The Koch arm back in its working pose with its torque on, the foam pad and blocks in place. No seed changes the scene.
fidelity: Koch v1.1 URDF meshes (convex hulls), axes, limits, masses, inertias; link_6's misplaced centre of mass is put at its mesh centroid; its gripper is one rigid body. Only the forearm, wrist and gripper collide with the upper arm, the base and the shoulder link. Unpowered joints: friction 0.03 N m per XL430, 0.012 per XL330 (dynamic 70 %), 0.02 N m s/rad, rotor inertia 0.005 and 0.002 kg m2: estimates. The torque cut is code, 1 s after both grippers close.
